title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement:
A **trie** (pronounced "try", from re**trie**val) is a tree-like data structure used to efficiently store and search a dynamic set of strings, most commonly for prefix-based lookups such as autocomplete.

Implement the `Trie` class:
- `Trie()` initializes the trie object.
- `insert(word)` inserts the string `word` into the trie.
- `search(word)` returns `true` if `word` was previously inserted into the trie (as a complete word), and `false` otherwise.
- `startsWith(prefix)` returns `true` if any previously inserted word has `prefix` as a prefix, and `false` otherwise.

examples.explanation: insert("apple"); search("apple") -> true; search("app") -> false ("app" was never inserted as a complete word); startsWith("app") -> true ("apple" starts with "app"); insert("app"); search("app") -> true.

constraints: word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith.
hints: Checking a list of all inserted words against every search/startsWith call would be slow once many words are stored — you need a structure where shared prefixes share work.
Think of each node representing one character; a word is a path from the root. Nodes can have up to 26 children (one per letter) and a flag marking 'a word ends here'.
`search` needs to walk the path AND check the end-of-word flag on the final node; `startsWith` only needs the path to exist — the flag doesn't matter.

solution.approach: Represent the trie as a tree of nodes, where each node holds a map/object of child nodes keyed by character, plus a boolean flag marking whether a complete word ends at that node. `insert(word)` walks the tree one character at a time, creating child nodes as needed, and marks the final node's flag `true`. Both `search` and `startsWith` walk the same way and fail fast (return false) the moment a required character link doesn't exist — the difference is that `search` additionally requires the final node's end-of-word flag to be set, while `startsWith` only cares that the path exists. Sharing structure this way means every word with a common prefix reuses the same nodes, so lookups only cost as much as the length of the string being checked, regardless of how many words are stored.
solution.timeComplexity: O(L) for insert, search, and startsWith, where L is the length of the word/prefix being processed — each does one pass over its characters.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(N * L) in the worst case, where N is the number of inserted words and L is their average length, since each new word may add up to L new nodes.

title: Word Search II
statement:
Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and a list of strings `words`, return all words from `words` that can be constructed from letters of sequentially adjacent cells, where adjacent cells are horizontally or vertically neighboring. The same letter cell may not be used more than once within a single word.

Words may be returned in any order — this judge sorts the results before comparing, so the order your code produces doesn't matter.

examples.explanation: "oath" and "eat" can each be traced through adjacent cells; "pea" and "rain" cannot.
No path visits the cells in that letter order without reusing a cell.

constraints: board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter.
words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Searching for each word independently with a fresh DFS over the whole board works, but with many words it repeats the same board exploration over and over — most words share prefixes.
Combine all the words into a single trie first. Then do one DFS pass per starting cell, walking the trie and the board in lockstep — a path with no matching trie edge can be abandoned immediately.
Whenever a DFS path lands on a trie node marked 'end of word', you've found a match. Mark visited cells (e.g., temporarily overwrite them) so a word can't reuse a cell, and restore them on backtrack.

solution.approach: Build a trie out of every word in `words` so that shared prefixes share the same search work. Then, for every starting cell on the board, run a DFS that walks the board and the trie simultaneously: at each step, look up the current board character as a child edge of the current trie node — if that edge doesn't exist, the path can't spell any remaining word and the DFS backtracks immediately (this is what makes the combined-trie approach far faster than searching each word from scratch). Whenever the DFS reaches a trie node flagged as the end of a word, record that word. Cells are temporarily marked visited (and restored after backtracking) so a single cell is never reused twice within the same word. Once a word is found, its end marker is cleared from the trie so it isn't reported again.
solution.timeComplexity: O(M * 4 * 3^(L-1)) where M is the number of board cells and L is the longest word — each cell starts a DFS that branches into at most 3 new directions per step (never back the way it came); building the trie first costs O(sum of word lengths).
solution.spaceComplexity: O(sum of word lengths) for the trie, plus O(L) recursion depth for the DFS.
